title: Best construction proposal software by contractor type
summary: Compare construction proposal software by contractor type, including Buildertrend, JobTread, PandaDoc and GetAccept, on tracking, signing and price.
body_markdown:
After a weekend spent poring over takeoffs and getting the scope just right, your proposal is finally ready to send. By Monday morning, it’s in the client’s inbox, but now comes the part that’s arguably more frustrating than putting it together: waiting to hear back.


The trouble is, you’ve no idea what’s happening on the client’s side. Has anyone opened it? Has the person holding the checkbook even seen it? Is the architect still working through the details? Without that visibility, following up becomes a guessing game.


Choosing the right[proposal software](https://www.getaccept.com/product/proposal-software) can change this. For most contractors, an all-in-one trade suite will do the job nicely. But when several people are involved in approving a bid, knowing what happens after you hit send becomes particularly valuable.


Although seeing who’s looked at your proposal won’t win you the contract on its own, it does give you a clearer sense of who to follow up with, when to reach out and what to discuss. This can be the difference between a promising bid that goes nowhere and a well-timed conversation that gets the contract over the line.


## What does construction proposal software do?


Construction proposal software builds the client-facing version of your estimate, which the client reviews and signs online. It’s typically the final stage of a three-step process:


- **Takeoff** : Measures quantities from the plans.
- **Estimate** : Calculates what those quantities will cost.
- **Proposal** : Presents the price and scope to the client for approval.


Some tools cover more than one step. A suite may run takeoff, estimate and proposal in one place, while a specialist handles a single step well. The important distinction is between the estimate and the proposal.


Whereas your estimate contains the internal cost calculations, your proposal is what the client ultimately agrees to – complete with your branding, scope of work, pricing, inclusions, exclusions, payment terms and a place to sign.


Once signed, it becomes the contract underpinning deposits, change orders and billing. So getting the details right matters every bit as much as getting the numbers right.


### How is bidding software different from proposal software?


Bid management tools help contractors invite subcontractors to submit quotes, compare those bids line by line (known as *bid leveling* ) and pull everything together into a consolidated bid for the project owner. This can help to limit the back-and-forth between contractors before a proposal reaches the client.


There *is* another wrinkle in heavy civil construction, where a “proposal” often means a formal bid submitted to a state Department of Transportation (DOT), rather than the client-facing document a remodeler might prepare.


Construction proposal software focuses on that final client-facing stage: presenting the scope, pricing and terms, and managing the proposal through to signature.


## What is the best proposal software for construction?


The best construction proposal software depends on your trade and how you manage bids. GetAccept is the best choice when a bid goes to several decision-makers, while trade suites such as Buildertrend, Houzz Pro and Procore fit contractors who want estimating and job management in the same tool.


Ultimately, your trade, team size and whether you need takeoffs will help narrow things down. Here’s how the main options compare, based on vendor information as of November 2026.


### Proposal software for residential builders and remodelers


Homeowner projects involve a number of moving parts, from material selections and change orders to clients who understandably want to know exactly what they’re paying for.


- **Buildertrend and JobTread** : Turn estimates into proposals, then help manage the job once everything’s signed.
- **Houzz Pro** : Includes takeoffs and tracks whether proposals have been sent, approved or declined.
- **BuildBook** : Lets clients approve web-based proposals online, with a full history of edits.


### Takeoff and proposal software for subcontractors and heavy civil


For subcontractors, preparing the numbers and presenting the bid are often two separate jobs. Dedicated takeoff tools handle the measurements, while proposals bring everything together for the client.


- **STACK and Procore** : Commercial construction tools covering takeoffs, estimating and bid preparation or management.
- **HCSS HeavyBid** : Built for heavy civil contractors, with standardized, branded bids covering inclusions, exclusions and qualifications.


### Proposal apps for specialty trades and small contractors starting out


If you’re running a smaller team, getting a quote approved quickly often matters more than having a long list of features. Especially when you’re quoting between jobs.


- **Jobber** : Clients can approve quotes and pay deposits through a dedicated client hub.
- **QuoteIQ** : Offers good, better and best pricing options, plus satellite property measurements.
- **Joist** : Handles mobile estimates and invoicing for solo contractors.
- **Handoff** : Uses AI to generate proposals for remodeling projects.


### Proposal software for commercial contractors with a sales team


Commercial bids tend to pass through several readers: an owner, a project manager, an architect and a finance lead.


- **GetAccept** is the best proposal software for teams sending proposals to multiple stakeholders, with tracking that shows what each person reads and e-signatures meeting ESIGN Act and UETA requirements. It works alongside your existing estimating software and integrates with HubSpot, Salesforce and other popular CRMs. The tracking plan requires at least five users, and there’s no built-in estimating or takeoffs.


## What features should construction proposal software have?


Construction proposal software should build the proposal from your estimate, track what the client does after send and capture legally binding signatures. Those are the three things worth judging each tool on, with particular attention to what happens after you hit send.


- **Tracking and follow-up after send** : An “opened” alert only tells you someone looked. Knowing who opened it and what they read matters more when an owner, project manager and architect are all reviewing your bid. GetAccept proposal software tracks each stakeholder’s views and time spent per section, with alerts for views, signatures and newly invited colleagues. So instead of chasing an update blindly, you can follow up on the details they’ve been looking at. Automated reminders keep things moving until signing, while CRM syncing gives your team a shared record of activity.
- **Built from your estimate** : Ideally, nobody should be copying figures between systems and hoping nothing gets missed. Construction suites typically pull line items directly from estimates, while standalone tools use uploaded PDFs or pricing tables. Either approach can work, but ask what happens when the estimate changes. Does the proposal update automatically, or is someone rebuilding it?
- **E-signature** : In the US,[electronic signatures](https://www.getaccept.com/learning-hubs/electronic-signature) need to meet ESIGN Act and UETA requirements. Look for timestamped audit trails and identity checks.


When you’re watching a demo, three questions should help separate the genuinely useful tools from the ones with impressive-looking dashboards:


- Can I see exactly who viewed the proposal, rather than just an “opened” notification?
- Can I see how long they spent reviewing individual sections, particularly exclusions?
- Will I have a record of who signed, when and from where?

## Can proposal software help with scope and change order disputes?


Few conversations are more frustrating for a contractor than a client questioning why something costs extra when work is already underway. In that circumstance, a clearly written, signed proposal is especially valuable. With inclusions and exclusions agreed upfront, you’ve got something concrete to refer back to when a change order comes up. When the client asks why a line item costs extra, the contractor points to the page where it was excluded.


Proposal tracking can also help you spot these potential misunderstandings before they happen. If a client spends a minute reviewing your pricing but barely glances at the exclusions, you have reason to believe they may need that conversation again before work starts.


The question is whether you can get that kind of visibility without replacing the construction software you already use.


## Can you use a general proposal tool instead of a construction platform?


Yes, a general proposal tool, such as GetAccept, works when your estimate already lives in a trade tool and you need to track and sign the proposal.


That’s how[Qwilr](https://www.getaccept.com/blog/qwilr-alternatives) positions its construction offering, for example. Your estimating and takeoff software handles the numbers; Qwilr handles the presentation.


The real advantage comes once you’ve sent the proposal.[PandaDoc](https://www.getaccept.com/blog/pandadoc-alternatives) offers detailed recipient analytics on its Business plan ($49 per user/month, billed annually, as of November 2026), while Qwilr tracks time spent on individual sections.


Both give you more to work with than a simple ‘opened’ notification, especially when several people are reviewing the same bid.


For commercial contractors who already have a dedicated estimating tool, this can be a sensible arrangement; but there are a few practical limitations to consider:


- **No native estimate sync** : You’ll need to transfer pricing using a PDF upload or pricing table.
- **Change orders stay in your construction suite** : The proposal tool won’t manage these.
- **Billing stays there, too** : Invoicing and payments remain part of your existing job workflow.

Which raises the question: how legally reliable are those signatures?


## Are e-signatures on construction proposals legally binding?


Yes. In the US, an electronic signature on a construction proposal can be just as legally binding as one made with pen and paper.


The ESIGN Act establishes that contracts can’t be denied legal effect simply because they’re electronic \[[Cornell University, 2026](https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/15/7001) \]. There are exceptions, including wills, certain family law matters and notices, but construction contracts aren’t among them.


State laws also come into play. Every state except New York has adopted a version of the Uniform Electronic Transactions Act (UETA), while New York has its own legislation \[[New York Bar, 2026](https://www.nycbar.org/issues-policy/advocacy-campaigns/ueta-esra-new-york-electronic-transactions-law/) \]. Under UETA, both parties must agree to transact electronically. And where written consumer notices are legally required, homeowners may need to receive specific disclosures and provide electronic consent under ESIGN.


When choosing software, look for two things:


- **An audit trail** : Evidence of who signed, when and from where.
- **Identity verification** : A way to confirm the person signing is who they claim to be.


[GetAccept complies with ESIGN and UETA](https://www.getaccept.com/product/electronic-signatures) and maintains a court-admissible evidence log. Keep this alongside your signed proposal in case questions arise later.


Of course, this is general information rather than legal advice. For guidance on your specific contracts, consult a qualified lawyer.
